content.text: The European Union will move to eliminate all tariffs on U.S. industrial imports and expand access for American farm products, part of an effort to shield European automakers from steeper duties on their exports to the U.S.

main.text: E.U. to Scrap Duties on U.S. Industrial Goods as It Scrambles to Soften Auto Tariff Blow

content.text: E.U. to Scrap Duties on U.S. Industrial Goods as It Scrambles to Soften Auto Tariff Blow The European Union will move to eliminate all tariffs on U.S. industrial imports and expand access for American farm products, part of an effort to shield European automakers from steeper duties on their exports to the U.S. The proposals follow a joint statement last week in which Brussels and Washington agreed to cut levies on European autos to 15% from a provisional rate of 27.5%. In return, the EU committed to lowering tariffs on a range of U.S. goods. "These proposals are the first steps in that implementation and ensure tariff relief by the U.S. for the vital EU automotive sector starting retroactively from Aug. 1," the European Commission, the bloc's executive arm, said Thursday. That suggests the lower auto tariffs are expected to be backdated to the beginning of the month, shortly after the two sides struck a deal that will see a baseline 15% tariff applied to European exports to the U.S. EU trade chief Maros Sefcovic said last week that U.S. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick has assured European officials of the retroactive application. Higher U.S. duties have rattled Europe's auto industry, with manufacturers from Jeep maker Stellantis to luxury-car maker Porsche reporting sharp declines in recent sales. Under the EU's proposal, tariffs on U.S. industrial goods would be scrapped entirely, while American seafood and certain non-sensitive agricultural products would receive preferential access to the European market. A separate proposal would extend tariff-free treatment for U.S. lobster, including processed varieties of the shellfish. The measures will now go to other EU institutions for approval. "These steps contribute to restoring stability and predictability in EU-U.S. trade and investment relations, the commission said. main.text: 欧盟将取消对美国工业产品的关税，努力减轻汽车关税带来的打击

content.text: 欧盟将取消对美国工业产品的关税，努力减轻汽车关税带来的打击 欧盟将采取行动，取消对美国工业品进口的所有关税，并扩大美国农产品的市场准入，此举旨在保护欧洲汽车制造商免受其对美出口产品被征收更高关税的影响。 这些提议是在布鲁塞尔和华盛顿方面上周发表联合声明之后提出的，双方在声明中同意将对欧洲汽车征收的关税从27.5%的临时税率下调至15%。作为回报，欧盟承诺降低对一系列美国商品的关税。 欧盟执行机构欧盟委员会周四表示：“这些提议是落实该协议的第一步，可确保美国为至关重要的欧盟汽车行业提供关税减免，并从8月1日起追溯生效。” 这表明，较低的汽车关税预计将追溯至本月初，即双方达成协议后不久。根据该协议，欧洲对美出口产品将被征收15%的基本关税。欧盟贸易专员马罗什?谢夫乔维奇(Maros Sefcovic)上周表示，美国商务部长霍华德?卢特尼克(Howard Lutnick)已向欧洲官员保证会追溯实施。 美国上调关税已对欧洲汽车行业造成冲击，从Jeep汽车制造商Stellantis到豪华车制造商保时捷(Porsche)等厂商均报告近期销量大幅下滑。 根据欧盟的提议，对美国工业品的关税将被完全取消，而美国海产品和某些非敏感农产品将获得进入欧洲市场的优惠准入。另一项提议将把对美国龙虾的免关税待遇扩大到包括该贝类产品的加工品种。 这些措施现在将提交给其他欧盟机构批准。 欧盟委员会表示：“这些举措有助于恢复欧盟与美国贸易和投资关系的稳定性和可预测性。” By Joshua Kirby; Write to Joshua Kirby at joshua.kirby@wsj.com; @joshualeokirby 版权所有(c)2025道琼斯公司。本文版权归道琼斯公司所有，未经许可不得翻译或转载。 (END) Dow Jones Newswires 28-08-25 1609GMT

main.text: Europe to Remove Duties on U.S. Industrial Goods to Get Lower Car Tariffs: Report

content.text: Europe to Remove Duties on U.S. Industrial Goods to Get Lower Car Tariffs: Report The European Union is prepared to remove all tariffs on U.S. industrial imports to the bloc in exchange for lower vehicle levies on EU exports to the States, according to a Bloomberg report. The European Commission, the executive arm of the EU which negotiates trade deals for its 27 member states, will get legislation through addressing industrial-goods tariffs by the end of the week, Bloomberg reported, citing people close to the matter. That would meet a key demand from President Donald Trump before his administration is willing to lower the rate that EU automakers face on cars sent to the U.S.—EU cars and parts are currently subject to a 27.5% U.S. tariff. Most goods are only subject to a 15% tax after the most recently negotiated trade deal, but Trump refused to apply that rate to cars until further demands were met. That could be good news for European brands like Porsche, BMW, Ferrari, and Volkswagen. While many European car makers already make cars within the U.S., the lighter import tax could have an impact on U.S. producers such as Ford, General Motors, and Stellantis. If the fast-tracked legislation gets through this month, then the 15% rate on European cars would be backdated to Aug. 1. Automobiles are one of Europe's biggest exports to the U.S. The EU will also give preferential tariff rates on some seafood and agriculture products, the Bloomberg report said. Trump has also railed against digital taxes on U.S. tech companies imposed by Europe but that doesn't appear to be a part of the deal. The EU Commission didn't immediately respond to a request for comment. Write to Brian Swint at brian.swint@barrons.com

main.text: $80-bn automobile components industry looks for path to steer around Trump wall

content.text: $80-bn automobile components industry looks for path to steer around Trump wall Gurgaon: Manesar, one of the three main engines alongside Chennai and Pune of India's massive automobile sector, is bracing for impact as the 50% tariff regime comes into effect. But unlike garment exporters, the auto ancillary industry does not have to contend with a blanket 50% tariff, giving it some wiggle room. Jagdeep Rangar of Stork Rubber Product, which makes engine mounts, rubber bushes, high voltage polymer insulators, etc, said auto component exports to the US can be categorised into two parts - supplies to light trucks and passenger vehicles, which have a 27.5% tariff and will continue to be so, and components for marine, agriculture (like tractors), heavy trucks, heavy machines and cranes that face a 50% tariff. Though it's the latter that will take the bigger hit, sources said the impact will be felt across ancillaries because the same companies often manufacture parts in both categories. "We are hoping to get some relief from govt, otherwise we will not be able to absorb the kind of discounts being demanded by buyers," said Rangar, adding finding new markets is not easy as developing a new product is a long process with a lead time of around two years. "Auto components are not developed overnight. We have to invest in tooling, send samples for testing. There are many more steps before the product is fit for the market," said Rangar, describing the current situation as "a flux". Vinnie Mehta, director-general of Automotive Component Manufacturers Association of India(ACMA), said auto components exports to the US in 2024 stood at $6.6 billion. "Of this, $3.5 billion worth of export will continue to be at 25%. This covers parts and components for cars and small trucks covered under US Proclamation 10908 dated March 26, 2025. This is about 55% of our export to the US. The remaining will attract a 50% tariff." India's automotive component industry is worth around $80 bn, out of which $23 bn is exports and the US share is around 8-9%, added Mehta. "It is too early to comment on the gravity of the impact. EU is also a $7-billion market." Nitin G R, founder of auto accessories maker GrandPitstop, said the company is trying to find ways to overcome the shock. "We are exploring ways to reach the US market with a lower tariff burden. Re-routing shipments through third countries is an option under consideration." An industry insider said many companies have already started work on diversifying their client base in other countries. "Indian companies are looking to expand in the Middle East, Africa and Latin America." Shradha Suri Marwah, president of ACMA, said: "While this development presents nearterm headwinds, it also underscores the importance of enhancingcompetitiveness, strengthening value addition, and exploring new markets."

main.text: German auto industry cuts over 51,000 jobs over U.S. tariff, weak demand: report

content.text: German auto industry cuts over 51,000 jobs over U.S. tariff, weak demand: report BERLIN, Aug. 26 (Xinhua) -- Germany's auto industry have cut more than 51,000 jobs over the past year as weak demand, U.S. tariffs and the costly shift to electric vehicles weighed heavily on the sector, according to a report by consultancy EY. Employment in the auto sector fell by nearly 7 percent over the 12 months to June, making it the hardest-hit branch of German industry, according to the report, quoted by the German press agency (dpa) on Tuesday. Across the broader industrial sector, headcount dropped by about 114,000 to 5.42 million, down 2.1 percent year-on-year. Actually, major automakers have reported significant profit declines. BMW, Mercedes-Benz and Volkswagen, Germany's three largest automakers, all reported steep profit declines in the first half of 2025, citing U.S. tariffs as a major drag on earnings. Hildegard Mueller, president of the German Association of the Automotive Industry (VDA), said the tariffs still impose billions of euros in added costs each year, a heavy burden as carmakers navigate the transition toward electrification. In 2024, Germany exported around 450,000 vehicles to the United States while German carmakers produced more than 840,000 vehicles at U.S. facilities, roughly half of which were exported globally, according to the VDA. This cross-border production model is particularly vulnerable to sudden policy changes. Macroeconomic indicators also signal weaker export momentum. The Ifo Institute has reported that export expectations in Germany deteriorated in August, falling to minus 3.6 points from minus 0.3 points in July. "Disillusionment is spreading in export business," said Klaus Wohlrabe, head of Surveys at Ifo. "Although a tariff rate of 15 percent from the U.S. is less than feared, it will nevertheless weaken export momentum." EY's Jan Brorhilker said "Severe profit declines, overcapacity and weakening foreign markets are making substantial job cuts unavoidable, especially in Germany, where management, administration and R&D are concentrated." Since early 2024, several automakers and suppliers, including Ford, Stellantis, Volkswagen, ZF and Bosch, have announced layoffs or plant closures in Germany and other European countries. In addition, shrinking order books, along with rising energy and labor costs, are eroding the region's industrial competitiveness. According to the Ifo Institute, more than one-third of companies report a shortage of orders, with the auto, machinery, and electrical equipment sectors hit particularly hard. Enditem
President Trump's tariff war has inflicted almost $12 billion of losses on global automakers, the biggest hit they have faced since the pandemic. The scary reality: This may be just the beginning.

main.text: Autos Take $12 Billion Hit From Trade War

content.text: Autos Take $12 Billion Hit From Trade War President Trump's tariff war has inflicted almost $12 billion of losses on global automakers, the biggest hit they have faced since the pandemic. The scary reality: This may be just the beginning. Beyond the continuing cost of tariffs, automakers in the U.S., Japan, South Korea and Europe face years of retooling and supply-chain tweaks to adjust to the new realities. This comes after they spent heavily to reshape factories for electric vehicles. The obvious responses to tariffs are to raise prices and move production to the U.S. But both are hard for carmakers to do quickly, potentially saddling them for years to come. Skeptics say the tariffs will change the industry only at the margins, with global automakers investing in the U.S. because of its healthy consumer economy, not its politics. Still, White House trade policy may be accelerating an industry trend toward making cars closer to where they are sold. The big auto markets of North America, Europe and China are increasingly divided by different regulations, technologies and consumer preferences, encouraging automakers to design and manufacture locally. "The era with globalization and global cars, everything equal -- that I think we are going to leave and have a world a bit more regionalized," said Hakan Samuelsson, chief executive officer of Volvo Cars. Toyota on Thursday said steeper tariffs reduced its operating profit by around $3 billion -- the largest bill reported by an automaker to date. The total hit from higher import duties reported by the big listed players now stands at $11.8 billion, according to a Wall Street Journal tally. And the hits will keep coming: Toyota forecast tariffs will create a $9.5 billion burden through its fiscal year that ends next March, leading to an anticipated 44% decline in net profit. For the world's 10 largest automakers, not including those in China, net profit is forecast to fall by roughly a quarter this calendar year to its lowest level since 2020, when the pandemic led to cash-draining factory shutdowns. When President Trump announced his 25% auto tariff in March, many analysts assumed that carmakers would increase prices to recoup the cost. It hasn't happened yet: The incentives typically used to clear inventory have thinned out, but most carmakers haven't rolled out headline price increases. Manufacturers need to balance the urge to protect their margins against the risk of lower sales if they deter consumers -- or of becoming a social-media target. "Nobody is in a rush to make a move before anyone else moves," Jefferies analyst Philippe Houchois said. "They're all afraid of getting a nasty tweet from Trump." General Motors said it expects "consistent pricing" to offset around 10% of its tariff costs this year, which it estimates at $4 billion to $5 billion, the largest of any auto manufacturer after Toyota. "At the end, it's about what will be the price that the customers will want the product at," Toyota Head of Finance Takanori Azuma said. The White House has also introduced policies that partly make up for the hit to profits, giving automakers further reasons to prolong the waiting game. Moves to unwind climate regulations spare Detroit the cost of increasing unprofitable EV sales or buying emissions credits -- at the expense of Tesla and Rivian, which profited from selling credits -- while giving the industry license to sell as many lucrative pickup trucks as it can. Ford said last week that it had already scaled back its purchases of regulatory credits by $1.5 billion. Trump's "Big Beautiful Bill" also allows many buyers of U.S.-made vehicles to deduct up to $10,000 in loan interest payments from their taxes, starting next year. The tariff response that Trump has made clear he wants to see from automakers is more U.S. production. Among the early responders, GM -- historically the top U.S. car importer -- is increasing production of its Chevrolet Silverado and GMC Sierra pickup trucks in Fort Wayne, Ind., and dialing down output in Canada. The company expects manufacturing adjustments to offset an additional 10th of its tariff costs for 2025.

content.text: 欧对美工业品关税 拟加快废除立法; 冀换降汽车关税 认贸协利美国 有指欧盟将加快废除美国工业品关税的立法程序，希望换取美国同意8月起降低汽车关税。欧盟承认贸易协议有利美国，但强调带来的稳定及确定同样重要。 彭博社周三（27日）引述消息人士报道，欧盟寻求在本周加快废除美国所有工业制品关税的立法程序，满足美国总统特朗普（Donald Trump）的要求，争取华府同意汽车关税下调至15%，8月起生效。 欧盟早前与美国达成贸易协议，同意几乎所有商品进口美国的关税可降至15%，但特朗普表明汽车关税下降，只会在欧盟提出废除工业品及其他关税的立法程序后实行。据悉欧盟亦向指定美国海鲜及农产品，提供优惠关税。 现时欧洲汽车及零部件的美国关税达27.5%，如欧盟成功在8月底前提出相关立法程序，美方将欧洲汽车关税降至15%，追溯期可至8月1日。汽车业为欧盟对美国最重要的出口行业，单是德国去年已向美国出口的新车及零部件价值高达349亿美元（约2,719亿港元）。 欧盟委员会主席冯德莱恩（Ursula von der Leyen）亦罕有发文，解释美欧贸易协议。她指协议坚固，但不完美，而协议核心是终止跨大西洋彼岸劳费心力的争端，为欧洲企业重新带回稳定及可预测性。 强调稳定确定同样重要 冯德莱恩指出，欧盟的报复性关税将有触发成本高昂贸易战的风险，将对欧洲工人、消费者及各行各业产生负面影响。惟她表明，在任何升级情况下，唯一不变的是美国政府的不可预测性及高关税。 另一方面，美国白宫贸易顾问纳瓦罗（Peter Navarro）周三（27日）接受《彭博社》专访时，批评印度总理莫迪（Narendra Modi）正为俄罗斯战争机器提供资金，更形容俄乌战争为「莫迪战争」（Modi’s war），因在一定程度上必须先经过新德里，才能通往和平之路。 纳瓦罗指控，印度透过折扣价购买俄罗斯石油，是帮助俄罗斯并损害美国，而美国又要资助乌克兰。他表示，美国所有人因印度的行径蒙受损失，包括消费者、企业及工人。印度的高关税让美国失去职位、工厂、收入和更高薪酬，又要为「莫迪战争」提供资金，连美国纳税人也蒙受损失。 系列名: 鸣谢: 资料提供:

main.text: 华轮威尔森：汽车关税降低影响“微小，但积极”

content.text: 华轮威尔森：汽车关税降低影响“微小，但积极” 欧盟与美国日前发表联合声明，公布了双方在7月达成的新贸易协议的具体细节。然而，华轮威尔森(Wallenius Wilhelmsen)表示，汽车关税降低影响“微不足道，但积极”。 具体而言，欧盟与美国在8月21日发表联合声明，公布了双方在7月达成的新贸易协议的具体细节。 美国将对汽车、药品、半导体和木材等大多数欧盟输美商品征收15%的关税。稀缺自然资源（如软木）、飞机及零部件、仿制药等得到豁免。 在公布与美国达成贸易协定的细节的同时，欧盟方面表示，未来将依据商定的框架和适用程序，与美国就一项公平、平衡且互利的贸易协定展开谈判。 Wallenius Wilhelmsen投资者关系与市场分析全球主管Anders Redigh Karlsen表示，美国已同意将从欧盟进口的汽车关税从27.5%降至15%，这将使汽车运输市场更具可预测性。 然而，对欧盟汽车征收15%的关税将不会生效，直到欧盟出台立法取消对美国商品的关税。 他指出，“现在的关税比去年高，现在就具体说明这可能对从欧洲到美国的汽车运输量产生什么影响还为时过早。” 他补充称，“然而，与最初宣布的关税相比，关税的下降尽管微小，但积极。达成框架协议达也提供了更多的可预测性。” 简言之，今年4月2日，即“解放日”，美国对进口乘用车和汽车零部件加征25%关税。此前的关税为2.5%。 尽管关税提高到27.5%，但Wallenius Wilhelmsen和挪威汽车船运营商礼诺航运（H?egh Autolines）都在二季度实现了强劲的业绩。 Wallenius Wilhelmsen表示，从亚洲到美国以外目的地的业务量大幅增加。另一方面，由于美国的关税，欧洲的出口量表现出克制和“观望”的态度。为了适应这一趋势，Wallenius Wilhelmsen已将运力从出口较弱的欧洲转移到中国出口市场。 特别值得一提的是，美国企业研究所高级经济学家瑞安·扬表示，美国最高法院很有可能在未来几个月推翻特朗普的全球关税，从而否定美国与欧盟贸易协定的部分内容。 他指出，这份协议的尴尬之处在于缺乏法律约束力。 “虽然每个人都希望关税能够保持稳定，但这项协议可能无法实现这一目标。”

main.text: Pune auto hub braces for Trump tariffs, seeks government relief

content.text: Pune auto hub braces for Trump tariffs, seeks government relief Industry leaders fear that the move could affect exports and disrupt operations, putting the livelihoods of nearly five lakh people engaged in the region's auto ecosystem at risk. Stakeholders are now urging both the State and Central governments to step in with supportive measures to help the industry navigate the challenge. Home to auto majors such as Tata Motors, Mahindra & Mahindra and Bajaj Auto, alongside global giants like Volkswagen and Mercedes, Pune is one of India's largest automobile clusters. Maharashtra alone accounts for 35.1 per cent of the country's automobile output by value. The Pimpri-Chinchwad belt, at the heart of this hub, houses over 4,000 manufacturing and ancillary units that keep the supply chain running. Industry associations are assessing the extent of the tariff's fallout. "We are gauging the impact US tariffs will have on industries in the region. We have been in discussion with all stakeholders, and we are confident industries will emerge stronger through this challenge," said Prashant Girbane, Director General of the Mahratta Chamber of Commerce, Industries and Agriculture (MCCIA). According to him, the forging sector within auto components is expected to be among the worst hit. The US market, once a major consumer of Indian forging products, may turn to Mexico and other suppliers. By contrast, the IT and IT-enabled services (ITES) sector has not yet reported any immediate impact. Industrialists are calling for urgent policy interventions to maintain competitiveness. A reduction in power tariffs, they argue, would help lower production costs and sustain the export competitiveness of Indian engineering goods in the global market. Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises (MSME) Federation is particularly anxious, warning that export declines could strain smaller players. It has urged the government to actively support diversification of markets, especially in Germany, Russia and other potential destinations, to offset the US shortfall. The stakes are high, given Maharashtra's significant role in India's automobile exports. The State contributes 49 per cent of the country's two- and three-wheeler exports, 27.4 per cent of motor vehicle and car exports, 22.3 per cent of auto components and parts and 11.6 per cent of auto tyres and tubes. Any disruption to this export engine could ripple through the economy. As the Pune auto cluster awaits clarity on the full scope of tariff impact, the industry's collective hope rests on swift government action to protect jobs, sustain manufacturing and open new global markets.

main.text: Stiff competition and Trump's tariffs sink global auto accounts

content.text: Stiff competition and Trump's tariffs sink global auto accounts As the saying goes, all's fair in troubled waters, but the truth is that in the automotive sector, few have come out on top in the first half of 2025. The first six months of the year have been marked by an all-out battle in China to stoke demand with aggressive discounting, the arrival on the scene of U.S. President Donald Trump's tariffs, and a race to dominate the electric vehicle that is not letting up. Of these three elements, the most disruptive has been the tariff, both because it was unexpected and because it has altered the foundations of an interconnected value chain that involves companies from several countries in the production of each car. The tariffs on European cars affect above all the German automobile industry, which sells a lot to the United States with brands such as Volkswagen, Audi, Mercedes-Benz and Porsche, but also indirectly affects countries such as Spain, which, although it does not sell complete vehicles to the United States, does make parts for German factories. As was foreseeable, the US tariffs, which for the time being remain at 27.5% -although Europe has already set in motion the necessary legislative process to withdraw a large part of the duties on US industrial products, an essential step for the US to reduce the tax on European cars to 15%-, has wrecked the profit and loss accounts of the German car manufacturers. Volkswagen, the world's second largest car manufacturer and Europe's largest, suffered a negative impact of 1.3 billion euros on its accounts due to the tariffs. Its net profit plummeted by 36.6% between January and June, to 4,005 million euros, a figure that compares with a 2024 that had already been bad in itself. Volkswagen is thus moving further and further away from Toyota, which holds firm as the world's most profitable automaker, with 1.5 trillion yen in net profit between January and June, comprising the fourth quarter of its previous fiscal year and the first quarter of the current one (the Japanese fiscal year began in April). That amount, which translates to some 8.75 billion euros, is 35.4% lower than the same period last year. Toyota, however, has taken an even bigger hit than Volkswagen because of Trump's tariffs. As the company reported in early August, the new duties will cost it 1.4 billion yen this fiscal year, i.e. the approximate profit of an entire quarter. The other representatives of the engine of the land of the rising sun have also suffered the impact of the tariffs, such as Honda, which reduced its net profit by 64% to 0.227 trillion yen, about 1,322 million euros at the current exchange rate. In an attempt to control damages, the Asian firm announced in April that it will transfer production of the Honda Civic hybrid from Japan to the USA, a model in great demand in the North American market. The car and motorcycle manufacturer made automotive headlines between late 2024 and early this year for its negotiations with Nissan and Mitsubishi to create what would have been the world's third largest automaker. However, the talks ran aground due to Nissan's refusal to agree to become another Honda brand, when what it wanted was a merger between equals. The truth is that Nissan, which changed its CEO on April 1 with the appointment of Mexican Iván Espinosa, went into the negotiations in a critical situation, which left it with few options: between January and June alone it lost 0.791 billion yen, some 4,613 million euros. The red numbers were particularly large between January and March, when it lost 0.67 billion yen.
